client: I've been really struggling lately with trying to keep my GPA up while also working part-time and somehow maintaining a social life at university. It feels like no matter how much I try, something always slips, and then I just spiral into this guilt about not doing enough. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the pressure is just... real, and I don't see how reframing my thoughts is going to make my workload any lighter.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now, and that exhaustion of constantly feeling like something's slipping no matter how hard you try makes complete sense given everything on your plate. You're right that reframing thoughts won't shrink your workload — and I want to be honest that CBT isn't about pretending the pressure isn't real, but more about exploring whether the *guilt spiral* on top of the stress is adding an extra weight we might be able to ease. I'm curious — when something does slip, what's the story you tend to tell yourself about what that means about you?

client: Honestly, when something slips, the story I tell myself is pretty brutal — like, it's proof that I'm not cut out for this, that I'm failing at work and probably letting everyone down at the same time. It's like one missed deadline or one forgotten thing becomes this evidence that I'm fundamentally not capable. And the worst part is I know it sounds extreme when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels completely true.
therapist: That moment of hearing yourself say it out loud and recognizing it sounds extreme — that's actually a really important crack of awareness, and it takes courage to notice that. What you're describing is a thinking pattern called *overgeneralization*, where one slip becomes a verdict on your entire worth and capability, which is an incredibly painful way to experience mistakes. I'd love to gently explore that "evidence" with you — when you think back, are there moments where something slipped but you *weren't* fundamentally incapable, where you actually recovered or managed more than you're giving yourself credit for?

client: I mean... yeah, I guess there have been times where I messed something up at work and it didn't end in complete disaster. Like last spring I sent out a report with some errors in it, and I was convinced I was going to get fired, but my manager just asked me to fix it and that was kind of it. But here's the thing — I don't know if that actually helps, because in the moment when I make a mistake now, those examples just don't feel real or relevant, like my brain just pushes them aside and goes straight to the worst version of things.
therapist: What you just described is so common and so frustrating — your brain has essentially developed a habit of filtering out the evidence that contradicts the worst-case story, almost like it's running a biased search that only returns the scary results. The report example is actually really significant though, because it happened *in reality*, even if it feels distant and unconvincing right now. I'm wondering — what do you think it would take for an example like that to feel real and relevant in those moments, or is there something that makes your brain want to hold onto the worst version instead?

client: I think part of me holds onto the worst version because it feels safer somehow, like if I expect the worst then I won't be caught off guard when it happens. With the report thing, even when my boss said it was good, I immediately thought "she's just being nice" or "she hasn't looked at it closely enough yet." It's like my brain won't let me actually land on the good evidence, it just bounces off it.
therapist: What you just named is really insightful — that holding onto the worst version feels like a form of protection, a way of staying in control of the disappointment before it can hit you. That makes a lot of emotional sense, even though it comes at a real cost, because it means good things can never fully land for you — your brain has a built-in deflector for positive evidence. I'm curious about that deflector — when your boss said the report was good and your mind went to "she's just being nice," what would it have meant to actually let yourself believe her?

client:
I think if I actually let myself believe her, it would mean I'm... good at something? And that feels really uncomfortable to sit with, almost more uncomfortable than assuming she was lying.

Because if I accept that I did something well, then I have to keep doing well, and what happens when I inevitably mess up? It feels safer to just never believe the good stuff so I don't have that far to fall.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really profound — the good news has actually become *threatening*, because accepting it means taking on the risk of losing it, and that feels more dangerous than just never having it at all. It's a kind of self-protection that makes complete sense given how brutal that inner voice is when things go wrong, but it also means you're essentially living in a permanent defensive crouch, bracing for a fall that may not even come. I'm wondering — what do you think that constant bracing is costing you, day to day?

client: That word "bracing" really hits me, because yeah, that's exactly what it feels like — like I'm always tensed up, waiting for something to go wrong with this friendship, even when things are actually okay between us. I think it costs me... being present, I guess? Like even when we're having a good conversation, part of me is already mentally rehearsing how I'll handle it when she eventually pulls away or gets tired of me. It's exhausting, honestly, and I hate that I can't just let myself enjoy having someone in my life without turning it into this constant threat assessment.
therapist: There's something really tender in what you're sharing — that even in a good moment with someone you care about, you're already half-gone, mentally preparing for a loss that hasn't happened. It makes so much sense that it's exhausting, because you're essentially grieving the friendship preemptively, paying an emotional cost for a pain that may never arrive. I'm curious — when you imagine actually staying *present* in one of those good conversations with her, what feels most scary about letting your guard down, even just a little?

client: I think what scares me most is that if I actually let myself be fully there, fully happy in that moment, then when she does pull away it'll hurt so much more. Like I'm trying to control the damage in advance by not investing too much. But even saying that out loud, I can hear how exhausting and kind of sad that is — I'm basically punishing myself before she gets the chance to.
therapist: That last line you said — "I'm punishing myself before she gets the chance to" — is one of the most honest and courageous things you've said today, and the fact that you can hear the sadness in it tells me a part of you is ready to question whether this strategy is actually working for you. You're essentially choosing a guaranteed smaller pain over the risk of a larger one, but in doing so you're making the loss feel inevitable even when it isn't — and you're missing the relationship you're trying so hard to protect. I wonder, has this way of pre-emptively pulling back actually ever stopped the hurt when someone did disappoint you, or did it just mean you were alone with the pain on top of everything else?

client: Honestly, that question kind of stopped me in my tracks, because I know the answer and I don't really like it. No, it never actually stopped the hurt — when my friend Sarah pulled away last year, I had already been distant for weeks, and when it finally happened I still felt completely gutted, just also kind of... empty and alone on top of it. So I guess I've been paying the price twice, but I kept telling myself it was somehow smarter or safer.
therapist: What you just recognized is really significant — that the strategy you've been trusting to protect you has actually been costing you twice, the loneliness of holding back *and* the grief when it ends anyway. There's something quietly heartbreaking about that, and I want to acknowledge how much honesty it takes to sit with the fact that a coping strategy you've relied on hasn't been keeping you safe the way you hoped. I'm wondering — now that you can see that pattern more clearly, what feels different about how you might want to approach things with this friend you mentioned, even in small ways?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me does see it now — like, I've been so focused on not getting hurt that I've basically been hurting myself the whole time anyway. But when I think about actually being more open with this friend, there's this immediate wall that goes up, like my brain just says "no, that's how you get burned." I want to try something different, I really do, but I honestly don't know if I trust myself to do it without either going too far or pulling back completely at the first sign of anything uncomfortable.
therapist: There's something really hopeful in what you just said — "I want to try something different" is not a small thing, and it matters that that desire is there even while the wall goes up. The fear of going too far or shutting down completely makes sense, but I wonder if we're setting up a kind of all-or-nothing test for yourself when really, openness doesn't have to be a leap — it can be a very small, deliberate step. What might the tiniest version of "a little more present" look like with this friend, something so small it feels almost too modest to count?

client: I guess... maybe just not checking my phone as much when we're together. Like, actually putting it face-down on the table instead of keeping it as this escape hatch. But even saying that out loud makes me nervous, because what if she notices and expects more from me, and then I freeze up anyway?
therapist: That idea of putting the phone face-down is actually a really meaningful and concrete step — and I love that you came up with it yourself, because it shows you already know what presence could look like, even if it feels scary. The worry that she'll notice and expect more is worth sitting with, because it's another version of that same pattern — turning a potentially good moment into a threat before it's even happened. I'm curious — if she *did* notice you were more present and felt warmly toward you because of it, what would that actually be like, rather than the freeze you're anticipating?
